title: Holy Saturday
hook: the quiet day; in the old vigil a new fire is lit in the dark

segments.voice: Yesterday, Good Friday: a Roman cross, and your line: it is finished. Today is the day in between.

The day after a funeral has its own kind of quiet. The flowers are still there, the casseroles in the fridge. Everyone has gone home. The Gospels give this day almost nothing. Jesus has been laid in a new tomb cut in the rock, a great stone rolled to the door. Luke says the women went home, prepared spices to anoint the body, "and rested the sabbath day according to the commandment." Matthew adds only that a guard is posted and the stone sealed. Nobody in the story knows what comes next. Today's word is the name of that silence.
screen: `THE DAY AFTER THE FUNERAL.` → `A STONE ACROSS THE DOOR.` → `THEY RESTED THE SABBATH.`

segments.voice: Holy Saturday. For most of the day, churches stay bare and quiet, no celebration yet: a day for waiting in grief. But Christians have also wondered where Jesus was that day. The Apostles' Creed says, in the Book of Common Prayer, "He descended into hell." The First Letter of Peter says he "went and preached unto the spirits in prison." Out of those lines grew an old picture, sometimes called the harrowing of hell. In the Orthodox Easter icon, Christ stands on the broken gates of death, pulling Adam and Eve up out of their tombs by the wrists. Christians read that line of the creed in more than one way: some as a descent to the dead, some as a way of saying he truly died. Then night falls, and something happens in the dark. In the old Easter Vigil, kept by Catholics, Anglicans, Lutherans and others, people gather outside, or at the back of a dark church, and a new fire is lit. From it, one tall candle is lit, the Easter candle, and carried in slowly while someone sings: the light of Christ. People light small candles from it, then from each other, until the whole dark church is glowing. In Orthodox churches, it happens near midnight. Every light goes out. The priest comes out holding a single flame and invites everyone to come and receive the light, and it passes from candle to candle through the crowd, out into the street. John's Gospel has a line for it: "And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not."
screen: `A DAY OF SILENCE AND WAITING.` · `HE DESCENDED INTO HELL.` · `A NEW FIRE IN THE DARK.` · `CANDLE TO CANDLE, INTO THE STREET.`

segments.voice: Turn off the lights around you, or close your eyes, and let the dark be dark for a while, not knowing what comes next. Near the end, turn on one small light, light a candle if it's safe, or simply open your eyes, and watch how much one flame changes a room. If you pray, welcome it as a sign of what Christians wait for; if you don't, just notice the difference.
Holy Saturday. The quiet day between the cross and Easter, which ends in the dark with a new fire. Today's word.
Your line: light in the dark. One flame, then a whole church. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: On Holy Saturday churches stay bare and quiet during the day; after dark churches in several traditions hold the Easter Vigil, lighting a new fire and the Easter candle and passing its flame from person to person, and Orthodox churches pass the light at midnight.

what a scholar hears: the creed's he descended into hell, and 1 Peter 3:19, lie behind the image of the harrowing of hell, painted in the Orthodox Easter icon.

notes: Easter Vigil described generically (new fire, Paschal candle, 'the light of Christ', candles passed). Confirm across Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran use.
Orthodox Paschal service: 'Come, receive the light' near midnight. Confirm; the Jerusalem Holy Fire ceremony is not mentioned.
Anastasis icon (Christ pulling Adam and Eve from their tombs) and readings of the descent clause (descent to the dead; Reformed readings as Christ's suffering or true death). Confirm the balance.
'One of the oldest services in the Christian year' for the Easter Vigil: widely stated; confirm.
Luke 23:56: the women prepared spices before the sabbath and rested on it. Confirm the paraphrase order.

Editor review (days 113-131): 'the text is silent' overstated: Matthew 27:62-66 tells of the guard and the sealed stone on that day, now said (hook and myth). 'The disciples are hiding' (not in the text for this day), 'a borrowed tomb' (Matthew 27:60: Joseph's own new tomb), 'the most important week', 'the quietest one of all', 'says it best' and 'one of the oldest services' (unsourced superlatives) cut; the hook no longer tells the listener what they know from grief.
